value.overview: The Grasshopper Sparrow is a small, ground-dwelling bird of open grasslands, savannas, prairies, and lightly grazed fields. It is recognized by its short tail, flat-headed profile, pale brown streaked back, and distinctive insect-like song. Unlike many sparrows, it often runs through vegetation rather than perching prominently. Most populations breed in North America and migrate south in winter, while some southern populations remain resident.
value.classification: The Grasshopper Sparrow belongs to the family Passerellidae, the New World sparrows. Its scientific name is Ammodramus savannarum, and several geographic subspecies are recognized.
value.identification: This sparrow is about 11–13 cm long, with a relatively large bill, short tail, and rounded or flat-looking head. The upperparts are buffy brown with fine streaking, while the underparts are pale and usually unstreaked. A yellow-orange spot occurs at the front of the face near the eye, and the throat may show a small yellowish area. It is often difficult to see because it stays low in grass and moves quietly on the ground.
value.rangeHabitat: Grasshopper Sparrows breed mainly across the United States, southern Canada, Mexico, and parts of the Caribbean and Central America. Northern and temperate populations migrate south after breeding. In Costa Rica, the species is regarded as an uncommon to rare seasonal visitor, with records associated mainly with the nonbreeding period and open, grassy habitats. Suitable areas include dry savannas, pastures, agricultural clearings, and other low, sparse grasslands rather than dense forest.
value.migrationStatus: Migratory in much of its range. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly as an uncommon or rare winter visitor and passage migrant, especially during the dry season; it is not generally considered a common resident.
value.breeding: Breeding pairs usually occupy open grassland with scattered low vegetation and bare ground. The female builds a concealed cup nest on or close to the ground, often with a partial grass canopy or a side entrance. A typical clutch contains several pale eggs marked with brown or reddish spots. The female does most incubation, while both adults generally help feed the young. The species may raise more than one brood where conditions are favorable.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of insects during the breeding season, including grasshoppers, crickets, beetles, caterpillars, and other arthropods. Seeds become more important during the nonbreeding season. Grasshopper Sparrows usually forage on the ground, walking or running through short vegetation and searching among plant stems and leaf litter. They may make short flights to capture prey but generally avoid dense vegetation.
value.behavior: This is a secretive, mostly terrestrial sparrow that often freezes or crouches when approached and then runs before flying a short distance. Males sing from low perches, grass stems, or fence posts, producing a brief buzzy song resembling an insect. Outside the breeding season, individuals may occur alone or in small loose groups. Their subdued plumage and ground-level habits can make them easy to overlook, particularly in Costa Rica where they are not common.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population trend is decreasing, with declines especially associated with the loss and degradation of suitable grassland habitat.
conservation.threats: Major threats include conversion of native grasslands to cropland or development, intensive grazing, encroachment by shrubs and trees, inappropriate fire regimes, and degradation of wintering habitat. Pesticide use may reduce insect prey, while mowing or burning during the nesting season can destroy nests and young.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore native grasslands, savannas, and lightly grazed open habitats across both breeding and wintering ranges. Use rotational grazing and carefully timed mowing or prescribed burning to avoid the nesting season. Retain patches of sparse vegetation and bare ground, reduce unnecessary pesticide use, and support monitoring of seasonal migrants in Costa Rica and elsewhere.
